title: The great Buddha of Nara
hook: an emperor asks everyone, down to a handful of earth, to help cast a giant bronze Buddha

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japan: a gilt bronze Buddha from Korea, a divided court, and Prince Shotoku. Your line was the teaching arrives. What new thing did you give a fair hearing? Day nine hundred twenty-five.

The doors of the hall swing open, and at first the eyes don't know what they're looking at. A bronze knee, higher than your head. A hand raised, palm out, bigger than a person. Far above, in the dim light, a calm face looking down over everyone who walks in. Schoolchildren crane their necks. Deer wander outside the gate. This is Todaiji, in Nara, and the seated figure inside is the great Buddha. Today, Vairocana, and the strange invitation that made it.
screen: `A KNEE HIGHER THAN YOUR HEAD.` → `A CALM FACE FAR ABOVE.` → `TODAIJI, IN NARA.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. Japan's official chronicle, the Shoku Nihongi, preserves Emperor Shomu's edict calling for the image. He says he has the wealth and the power of the land, and could simply order it made. But that, he says, would miss the point. So he asks that anyone who wishes to help, even by bringing a single branch of grass or a handful of earth, be allowed to share in the work. A giant made of countless small offerings. Second, which Buddha. The great Buddha is Vairocana, called Rushana in Japanese, the Buddha at the center of the Flower Garland Sutra. That's the same sutra behind the Huayan school, the one Uisang carried home to Korea. In Japan it's called Kegon, and Todaiji became its great temple. In that sutra, Vairocana's light reaches into every world. A Buddha that large is trying to show something that large. Third, the opening of the eyes. When the image was finished, a ceremony was held to open its eyes, with an Indian monk, Bodhisena, holding the brush. Cords tied to the brush ran out into the crowd, so that many hands could hold them and share in the moment. Fourth, the face. Fire and war have damaged the image more than once, and the head you see today is a later recasting, not the first one. Through every repair, the expression stayed the same kind: not triumphant, calm. Vast things can be frightening: the sea at night, the sky over a desert. Here, vastness is shown at peace, a hand raised as if to say, don't be afraid.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF EARTH.` · `VAIROCANA OF THE FLOWER GARLAND.` · `CORDS TO THE BRUSH.` · `VASTNESS AT PEACE.` · then, large: `VAST AND CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture something vast. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the biggest thing you've ever stood in front of: an ocean, a mountain, a night sky, a cathedral ceiling, a canyon. Let it fill your inner sight. Notice the body's first response, a tightening or a widening. Then see if you can let it be calm, the way the bronze face is calm. Big, and at rest. Breathe inside that size for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Vairocana. The great Buddha of Nara, cast in bronze at Todaiji with the help of anyone who brought a handful of earth, vast and at peace. Today's word.
Your line: vast and calm. Today, look up at the sky once, on purpose, for one full breath, and let something that big be calm. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Todaiji in Nara is still a working temple of the Kegon school, where pilgrims and visitors come to bow before the great Buddha, and monks hold regular services in the hall.
